title: How the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World Works, Part II
summary: Part two of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World series. Covers the Statue of Zeus at Olympia (Phidias, ivory and gold, later moved to Constantinople and lost in a palace fire), the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus (Mausolus and Artemisia, five sculptors, later reused by the Knights of St. John and parts in the British Museum), the Colossus of Rhodes (Chares of Lindos, built after a Macedonian siege, toppled by earthquake about 54 years later, scrap sold by Arab invaders), and the Lighthouse of Alexandria (Pharos, Sostratus of Cnidus, fell in an earthquake around 1303). Also includes a sponsor-style opening promo for tour dates, a break, and a listener mail about bath salts (dangerous drug experience at a festival). Hosts note an earlier factual error in a source about the Statue of Zeus height.
topics: Seven Wonders of the Ancient World

segments.title: Statue of Zeus at Olympia
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Statue of Zeus at Olympia, made by Phidias of ivory and gold over a wooden core, housed in a sixty-eight-foot temple. They discuss the statue's seated pose, the Nike figure, its ties to coins, and its move to Constantinople where it was lost in a palace fire. Legend of a lightning bolt is dismissed.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break before the next wonder.

segments.title: Mausoleum at Halicarnassus
segments.summary: Story of King Mausolus and his sister-wife Artemisia, who commissioned the mausoleum; five sculptors and architect Pythius worked on it after her death. The structure was about 140 feet tall. It survived the abandonment of the city, was toppled by an earthquake, and parts ended up in the Knights of St. John's castle and the British Museum.

segments.title: Colossus of Rhodes
segments.summary: After a Macedonian siege of over a year, Rhodians left behind war machines that were reused as scaffolding and sold to fund a bronze and iron statue by Chares of Lindos, about 110 feet tall, possibly modeled on Alexander the Great and thanking Helios. It fell in an earthquake about 54 years later, stayed as a tourist attraction, and its remains were sold for scrap in 653 AD.

segments.title: Lighthouse of Alexandria (Pharos)
segments.summary: The Lighthouse of Alexandria on the island of Pharos was built around 280 BC, reportedly about 450 feet tall, at a cost of about 800 talents, with architect Sostratus of Cnidus. It used a polished reflector by day and a fire by night, and had internal ramps and hoists. It stood until earthquakes in 1303 destroyed it, and underwater blocks have since been found.

segments.title: Wrap-up of the Seven Wonders and wreck diving tangent
segments.summary: Hosts reflect on the connections among the wonders and the lighthouse's lasting economic value, then briefly discuss the Andrea Doria wreck and a future episode idea.

segments.title: Listener mail: bath salts
segments.summary: A listener describes taking what they believed was Molly at a festival, which turned out to be bath salts, causing numbness, paranoia, and sleeplessness. The hosts respond with advice to steer clear.
